'''Reginald Howard White''' (December 19, 1961 – December 26, 2004) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 15 seasons. White played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]], earning [[unanimous All-American]] honors. After playing two seasons for the [[Memphis Showboats]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL), he was selected in the first round of the [[1984 NFL supplemental draft of USFL and CFL players|1984 NFL Supplemental Draft]], and then played for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], the [[Green Bay Packers]] and the [[Carolina Panthers]], becoming one of the most awarded defensive players in NFL history.

The two-time [[NFL Defensive Player of the Year]], [[Super Bowl XXXI]] champion, 13-time [[Pro Bowl]], and 13-time [[All-Pro]] selection holds second place all-time among [[List of NFL career sacks leaders|NFL career sack leaders]] with 198. He was selected to the [[NFL 75th Anniversary All-Time Team]], [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]], [[NFL 1990s All-Decade Team]], and the [[NFL 1980s All-Decade Team]]. During his professional career, White is credited with pioneering [[free agency]] in sports. Outside of football he was also known for his Christian ministry as an ordained [[evangelical]] minister, leading to his nickname, "'''the Minister of Defense'''".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=March 13, 2013 |title=Top 5 NFL free agent signings |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/video/2013/03/13/top-5-nfl-free-agent-signings |access-date=March 16, 2026 |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]]|type=video}}</ref> White is a member of the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]].

'''Reuben Droughns''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|d|r|oʊ|n|z}}; born August 21, 1978) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). After playing [[college football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]], he was selected by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the third round of the [[2000 NFL draft]]. During his nine years playing professional football, Droughns was also a member of the [[Miami Dolphins]], [[Denver Broncos]], [[Cleveland Browns]], and [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He earned a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the Giants in their [[Super Bowl XLII]] victory against the [[New England Patriots]].

Following his playing career, Droughns worked as an assistant coach for the Serbian team [[Vukovi Beograd]],<ref name="l998">{{cite web | title=Ex-Browns RB Reuben Droughns heads overseas to coach in the CEFL | website=cleveland.com | date=2010-05-27 | url=https://www.cleveland.com/ohio-sports-blog/2010/05/ex-browns_rb_reuben_droughns_h.html | access-date=2024-10-15}}</ref> the two-time champions of the [[Central European Football League]] (CEFL) from 2010 to 2013.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.european-league.com/article/385/2010-vukovi.html|title = 2010: Vukovi » Central European Football League - CEFL|date = April 4, 2010}}</ref>

'''Reginald Wayman Wilkes''' (born May 27, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and [[Atlanta Falcons]].  He attended university and played [[college football]] at [[Georgia Institute of Technology|Georgia Tech]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science]]. Wilkes was selected by the Eagles in the third round of the [[1978 NFL draft]].

Wilkes was all-state at Southwest Atlanta High School and won the 1973 Georgia AA State Championship, heading a defense that allowed 126 yards rushing for the whole season. He went on to letter for Georgia Tech football all four years of college. Upon graduation, he was granted membership into the prestigious ANAK Society, Georgia Tech's honor society, which recognizes exemplary student leaders.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://anak.gtorg.gatech.edu/| title=The ANAK Society, Georgia Institute of Technology}}</ref>

In his rookie NFL year with the Eagles, Wilkes recorded 88 tackles, and along with [[Pro Bowler]] [[Bill Bergey]], co-led the team with five fumble recoveries.  He was named to the [[United Press International|UPI]] and [[Pro Football Weekly]] All-Rookie teams in 1978–79.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/Story-WhereAreTheyNow.asp?story_id=18710| title=Where Are They Now: LB Reggie Wilkes|work=[[Philadelphia Eagles]]|date=September 12, 2009}}</ref>  Wilkes played in every regular season game in his first three NFL seasons, and was a starting outside linebacker on the 1980–81 Philadelphia Eagles [[Super Bowl XV]] team.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/players/reggiewilkes/profile?id=WIL080775| title=NFL.com Stats|work=[[National Football League]]|accessdate=December 12, 2010}}</ref> After eight seasons with the Eagles, Wilkes finished his career with two years on the Atlanta Falcons. During his ten seasons in the NFL, Wilkes scored just one point; in a game against the [[New Orleans Saints]] on October 11, 1981, he caught a pass from [[Ron Jaworski]] for a successful [[point after touchdown]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Philadelphia Eagles at New Orleans Saints - October 11th, 1981 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198110110nor.htm |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |access-date=26 March 2026}}</ref> In 1989, Wilkes was inducted into the Georgia Tech Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ramblinwreck.cstv.com/ot/fame/halloffame.html#fbc| title=Georgia Tech Athletics Hall of Fame|work=[[Georgia Institute of Technology]]|accessdate=December 12, 2010}}</ref>  In 2013, Wilkes was inducted into the [[Georgia Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.macon.com/2013/02/23/2368333/new-class-of-five-enters-georgia.html|title=2013 Georgia Sports Hall of Fame inductees|work=[[The Telegraph (Macon)|The Telegraph]]|date=February 23, 2013}}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

During his 10-year NFL career, Wilkes worked on the staff of [[Merrill Lynch]] advisory group in the off-seasons.  Following his retirement from the NFL in 1988,  Wilkes and two partners began a registered investment advisory firm, Pro Cap, which specialized in investment and lifestyle management services for professional athletes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/2006/09/08/nfl-player-finances-cx_tvr_0910nfl.html|title=There's Gold In The NFL|work=[[Forbes]]|date=September 10, 2006|archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130123061925/http://www.forbes.com/2006/09/08/nfl-player-finances-cx_tvr_0910nfl.html|archivedate=January 23, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> They later sold that business to Mercantile Trust Bank, based in [[Baltimore]], and Wilkes maintained his position as senior vice president, heading up its sports and entertainment division. Wilkes returned to Merrill Lynch in 2007 and founded "The Wilkes Sports Management & Advisory Group", before moving to Janney Montgomery Scott, LLC, where he continues to specialize in wealth management of high-net-worth athletes in the [[NFL]] and [[NBA]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://advisor.janney.com/reginaldwilkes/our-team/| title=Reggie Wilkes, SVP, Janney Montgomery Scott, LLC}}</ref>

Wilkes, and his group, has been featured by numerous news and media outlets, including ''[[The New York Times]],'' <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/10/your-money/financial-lessons-from-sports-stars-mistakes-your-money.html?_r=1| title=Financial Lessons From Sports Stars' Mistakes|work=[[NY Times]]|date=September 10, 2011}}</ref> ''[[The Wall Street Journal]],'' [[Forbes]], [[U.S. News & World Report]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://money.usnews.com/money/retirement/aging/articles/what-former-pro-athletes-can-teach-you-about-saving-for-retirement| title=U.S. News, "What Former Pro Athletes Can Teach You About Saving for Retirement" |date=August 30, 2023}}</ref> [[CNBC]], [[Reuters]], ''[[Real Sports with Bryant Gumbel]]'',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hbo.com/real-sports-with-bryant-gumbel/index.html#/real-sports-with-bryant-gumbel/episodes/0/166-episode/index.html| title=HBO Real Sports, "Short Changed" |date=January 25, 2011}}</ref> and the documentary film ''Broke'', which premiered at the 2012 Tribeca/[[ESPN]] Sports Film Festival.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tribecafilm.com/news-features/TFF_2012_TFFESPN_Sports_Film_Festival.html#.T3HkDWB5Gkk|title=2012 Tribeca/ESPN Sports Film Festival, "Broke"|date=April 25, 2012|access-date=March 27, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315004529/http://www.tribecafilm.com/news-features/TFF_2012_TFFESPN_Sports_Film_Festival.html#.T3HkDWB5Gkk|archive-date=March 15, 2012|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref> The film is part of ESPN's ''[[30 for 30]]'' series of sports documentaries. Wilkes is a member of the [[NFL Alumni Association]] and is a [[NFLPA]] Registered Player Financial Advisor.

Wilkes operates offices in [[Philadelphia]] and [[Atlanta]] and lives with his wife in Philadelphia.

He became the team's full-time starter at tight end the following season.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Graham |first=Tim |date=2021-11-30 |title=Is Dawson Knox already the best tight end in Bills history? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2987837/2021/11/30/is-dawson-knox-already-the-best-tight-end-in-bills-history/ |access-date=2025-06-26 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Following his playing career, he returned to his hometown of Tulsa, Oklahoma and spent a decade at the Greenwood Chamber of Commerce.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tramel |first=Berry |title=Tramel: Former OSU football star Reuben Gant knows about the Tulsa Race Massacre now |url=https://www.oklahoman.com/story/sports/2021/05/30/osu-football-reuben-gant-now-knows-his-tulsa-race-massacre-history/5259828001/ |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=The Oklahoman |language=en-US}}</ref> He now serves as the executive director for the John Hope Franklin Center for Reconciliation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Board of Directors |url=https://www.jhfcenter.org/board |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=johnhopefranklin |language=en}}</ref>

Gant's career and life were profiled in a feature titled "Reuben Gant NFL and Community Champion"<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-22 |title=POSITIVELY OKLAHOMA: Reuben Gant NFL and Community Champion |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/positively-oklahoma-reuben-gant-nfl-004827428.html |access-date=2025-06-26 |website=Yahoo News |language=en-US}}</ref> on [[KJRH-TV|KJRH's]] ''Positively Oklahoma'' during Black HIstory Month in 2025.
